title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin ones, and a plan to store grain

segments.voice: Yesterday, dreams in prison: the butler got out and forgot. Your line: don't forget Joseph. It's the end of a week that began with Rachel's grave and ran through a coat, a pit, Tamar, Potiphar's house and a prison. Today, the door opens.

Two full years after the butler forgot, Pharaoh has a nightmare. He's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up, thin and ugly, and eat the seven fat cows. And they're still just as thin. Pharaoh wakes, falls back asleep, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. All the wise men of Egypt are called. Nobody can explain it. And suddenly the butler, standing right there, remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: They rush Joseph out of the dungeon. He shaves and changes his clothes, another change of garment in this story, and stands before Pharaoh. I hear you can interpret dreams, says the king. Joseph's first words: "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Not me. God. The two dreams are one, he explains. Seven good years are coming, years of plenty across Egypt. Then seven years of famine, so heavy that the plenty will be forgotten. The dream came twice because it's certain, and soon. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives Pharaoh a plan: find a wise man, collect a fifth of the harvest in the good years, store the grain in the cities, and when the famine comes, the country won't perish. Pharaoh looks around: who could be wiser than the man who just said this? Joseph goes from the prison to the palace, second only to Pharaoh. He's thirty years old. He was seventeen in the pit. He gets a ring, fine linen, a gold chain, an Egyptian name, and a wife. His two sons' names tell you what's inside him. Manasseh: God made me forget my hardship and my father's house. Ephraim: God made me fruitful in the land of my suffering. In the good years, Joseph stores grain beyond counting. When the barns are full, a famine is easy to forget. That's exactly when he gets ready.
screen: `IT IS NOT IN ME.` · `SEVEN OF PLENTY, SEVEN OF FAMINE.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `PRISONER TO SECOND IN EGYPT.` · then, large: `STORE IN THE GOOD YEARS.`

segments.voice: Think about what's plentiful in your life right now, money, time, energy, friends, patience, and pick one. Then picture a leaner season that might come, and one small thing you could store up for it now: a few dollars, a phone call to keep a friendship warm, a good night's sleep.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin: seven years of plenty, seven of famine, and a plan to store grain in the good years.
Your line: store in the good years. Reading the dream was the easy part. Seventy days now: ten whole weeks.

screen: `DAY 70 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BROTHERS COME FOR BREAD.`

howItsDone: Jews read this chapter in the weekly Torah portion Miketz, which the calendar often places during Hanukkah.

match.prompt: what's inside the dreams — tap the pairs.

myth: Joseph said he had a gift for reading dreams
"It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace."

he was seventeen when his brothers sold him. thirteen years passed.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. you've just explained Pharaoh's dreams. famine is coming. what do you do next?
options: bow and wait to be sent back to prison.
propose a plan to store grain.
ask to be sent home to your father.
fork.reveal: he proposes a plan: a wise man, a fifth of the harvest, grain stored in the cities. Pharaoh chooses him to run it.

original.note: Hebrew: plenty, being full. its opposite in the dream is ra'av, famine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who could read dreams.
what it means: a story about planning. reading the dream is the easy part; storing grain in the good years is the work.
what a scholar hears: Joseph's sons' names are wordplays: Manasseh from nashah, to forget; Ephraim from parah, to be fruitful.
guess: a warning: seven years of plenty, then famine
a sign that Pharaoh's reign would end soon
a curse on the Nile sent by Egypt's gods
